title: Interpretable Deep Learning Models for Breast Cancer Diagnosis Using Medical Imaging
authors: Sami Alnawali, Muhammad Atif Saeed, Abdul Hadi, Azka Atiq, Akhtar Jamil, Ahmad Din
abstract: Deep learning shows promise for breast cancer diagnosis, but limited interpretability hinders clinical adoption. We benchmark ten ImageNet-pretrained models (ResNet50, VGG19, InceptionV3, DenseNet121, Xception, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, ViT, and Swin Transformer) for benign-versus-malignant classification on the BreakHis histopathology dataset using a patient-level split, and explain their predictions with Grad-CAM, LIME, Integrated Gradients, and LRP. DenseNet121 performed best, with 99.4% test accuracy and an AUC-ROC of 0.999, and significantly outperformed all other models (p < 0.001). Transformer-based models trailed the CNNs. The explanations consistently highlighted nuclei-rich and glandular regions of diagnostic relevance. Combining transfer learning with explainable AI can thus yield accurate, interpretable tools for breast cancer diagnosis.

infographic.key_insight: DenseNet121 led ten pretrained models in classifying benign versus malignant breast histopathology images, achieving 99.4% test accuracy and 0.999 AUC-ROC.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Interpretable image classification could support breast pathology assessment, but these research results do not establish clinical readiness.
method: Benchmarked ten ImageNet-pretrained CNN and transformer models on BreakHis histopathology images.
Used a patient-level split for benign-versus-malignant classification.
Applied Grad-CAM, LIME, Integrated Gradients, and LRP; explanations highlighted nuclei-rich and glandular regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the BreakHis patient-level test split, DenseNet121 reportedly outperformed all other models (p < 0.001), while transformers trailed CNNs.
infographic.watch_item: External validation and prospective clinical evaluation are not reported in the abstract, leaving real-world generalizability uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Interpretable Deep Learning Models for Breast Cancer Diagnosis Using Medical Imaging

title: ClinVerse: A Realistic Multi-Agent Diagnostic Environment for Training and Evaluating Medical Agents
authors: Sirry Chen, Fangke Chen, Xuanwen Ding, Wei Chen, Zhongyu Wei
abstract: Disease diagnosis is a key application of large language model (LLM) agents in healthcare. However, existing medical agents are primarily trained and evaluated with static question-answering data, providing limited opportunities to learn active information acquisition, examination decision-making, and dynamic clinical interaction. To address this limitation, we present ClinVerse, an interactive, real-data-grounded multi-agent environment designed for training and evaluating medical diagnostic agents. Built on ClinPatient, a scalable dataset comprising 150k diagnostic cases derived from real-world electronic health records, ClinVerse supports coordinated interactions among six specialized clinical roles. Specifically, a doctor agent starts from an initial patient complaint, progressively gathers clinical evidence through patient interviews and examination requests, and ultimately produces a diagnosis. For each interaction trajectory, a rule-based scoring framework quantifies information acquisition, examination ordering, and diagnostic accuracy. These trajectory-level scores serve as reward signals for agent training while also enabling scalable evaluation. In experiments, we evaluate various general-purpose and medical-domain models and show that nine self-evolution methods across three categories consistently improve agents' diagnostic capabilities within ClinVerse. We further analyze the interplay among model capability, environment feedback, and self-evolution methods.

infographic.key_insight: ClinVerse moves medical AI training and evaluation beyond static questions into interactive diagnostic encounters with six specialized clinical roles.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The environment tests how agents gather patient information, request examinations, and reach diagnoses rather than assessing answer accuracy alone.
method: Ground simulated encounters in ClinPatient, a dataset of 150,000 diagnostic cases derived from real-world electronic health records.
Let a doctor agent interview patients and request examinations before producing a diagnosis.
Score information acquisition, examination ordering, and diagnostic accuracy to support training and evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across general-purpose and medical-domain models, the abstract reports that nine self-evolution methods in three categories consistently improved diagnostic capabilities within ClinVerse.
infographic.watch_item: Improvements within this simulated environment do not establish safety or effectiveness in real clinical practice.
infographic.paper_title: ClinVerse: A Realistic Multi-Agent Diagnostic Environment for Training and Evaluating Medical Agents

title: DocTalk: Enhancing Medical Knowledge Retrieval via Fine-tuned Large Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Robust Clinical Decision Support
authors: Asad Gohar, Md Ariful Islam Mozumder, Moon-Il Joo, Hee-Cheol Kim
abstract: Objective: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare has opened new possibilities for AI-assisted clinical decision-making; however, safe and effective deployment remains challenging because of hallucination and domain misalignment. This study introduces DocTalk, a doctor-assistive question-answering (QA) system designed to generate concise, chart-grounded responses from de-identified discharge summaries. Methods: We developed a high-fidelity data generation pipeline that produces 500 clinically relevant QA pairs through sentence-level decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review. Six open-source LLMs, including three general-purpose and three biomedical models, were evaluated before and after parameter-efficient instruction tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). The framework integrates prompt engineering, in-context learning, and medically aligned evaluation to support factual and interpretable responses. Results: On DocTalk-QA, instruction tuning produced consistent improvements across lexical, semantic, and clinical fidelity metrics. The best-performing tuned model, Llama-3-Med42-8B, achieved ROUGE-L = 0.40, BERTScore-F1 = 0.76, and UMLS-F1 = 0.49. To examine external generalization beyond the DocTalk-QA dataset, the two best-performing models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3-Med42-8B, were evaluated on PubMedQA before and after instruction tuning. Accuracy improved from 0.931 to 0.977 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from 0.935 to 0.943 for Llama-3-Med42-8B. Conclusion: DocTalk was deployed as a secure web-based platform for interactive EHR querying. These findings suggest that clinically grounded instruction tuning can improve medical QA performance and support practical clinical decision support.

infographic.key_insight: DocTalk’s chart-grounded instruction tuning improved medical question-answering performance across six open-source language models.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The system could help clinicians retrieve information from discharge summaries, but the abstract does not establish benefits for patient care.
method: Generated 500 QA pairs from de-identified discharge summaries using sentence-level decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review.
Evaluated three general-purpose and three biomedical models before and after LoRA instruction tuning.
Tested the two best-performing models on PubMedQA for external generalization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The best tuned model achieved ROUGE-L 0.40, BERTScore-F1 0.76, and UMLS-F1 0.49; PubMedQA accuracy improved from 93.1% to 97.7% and 93.5% to 94.3% for the two evaluated models.
infographic.watch_item: The small, generated QA dataset and benchmark results do not establish real-world clinical safety or reliable hallucination control.
infographic.paper_title: DocTalk: Enhancing Medical Knowledge Retrieval via Fine-tuned Large Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Robust Clinical Decision Support

title: MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One Decision Making in Medicine
authors: Simon A. Lee, Jiahang Sha, Moonseong Jeong, Yunbei Pan, Jeffrey N. Chiang
abstract: System One decision models such as Jev answer structured questions in a single forward pass without generating text, offering fast and computationally efficient clinical decision support. We evaluate MedJev, an open System One model that runs locally on a laptop, across ten medical benchmarks spanning medical knowledge, diagnosis, and patient level prediction using MIMIC IV and MIMIC IV ED. We compare MedJev against zero shot LLM baselines, published GPT results, and supervised models. MedJev achieves accuracies of 72.5 percent on MedQA, 75.4 percent on USMLE, and 80.1 percent on NEJM, approaching published GPT 4 performance while maintaining well calibrated confidence estimates (ECE 0.028 to 0.063). On patient level tasks, MedJev achieves an AUROC of 0.926 for In Hospital Mortality, exceeding XGBoost (0.902), but underperforms supervised models on operational outcomes such as ED Triage Admission (0.745 vs. 0.809). Patient level predictions also exhibit substantial miscalibration (In Hospital Mortality ECE 0.286). We introduce a lightweight, two parameter recalibration method that adapts predictions to local patient populations using 50 to 200 labeled examples, reducing ECE to 0.007. Our findings establish open System One models as a promising zero shot baseline for medical AI, combining competitive predictive performance with low computational cost and efficient local calibration. We release our code and evaluation harness to support future research.

infographic.key_insight: MedJev delivers competitive zero-shot medical predictions in a single forward pass, but patient-level confidence estimates require local recalibration.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Laptop-based inference could support low-compute clinical decision research, though benchmark performance does not establish safety or benefit in clinical practice.
method: Evaluated an open System One model across 10 medical benchmarks without generating text.
Compared zero-shot predictions with LLM baselines, published GPT results, and supervised models.
Tested two-parameter local recalibration using 50–200 labeled examples.
infographic.evidence_signal: MedJev achieved 72.5% MedQA accuracy and 0.926 in-hospital mortality AUROC on MIMIC-based evaluation; reported recalibration reduced mortality expected calibration error from 0.286 to 0.007.
infographic.watch_item: Performance varied by task: ED admission AUROC lagged a supervised comparator (0.745 vs. 0.809), and strong discrimination did not ensure reliable confidence estimates.
infographic.paper_title: MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One Decision Making in Medicine

title: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis
authors: Roxana Ramona Szomiu, George Ursu, Adrian Groza
abstract: Effective differential diagnosis depends on well structured and unambiguous patient case descriptions, since incomplete or ambiguous clinical information readily leads to diagnostic errors and inconsistent reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in medical question answering and clinical reasoning; however, even when achieving competitive performance on medical benchmarks, they often rely on pattern recognition learned from training data rather than grounded clinical evidence, and can generate plausible yet unsupported diagnostic conclusions. Their reasoning remains largely opaque, making it difficult for clinicians to assess the evidence and rationale behind a given recommendation. To address this gap, we propose an ontology-guided, multiagent differential diagnosis framework that replicates the iterative reasoning process of physicians. The framework grounds diagnostic inference in a structured, expert-curated medical knowledge base, enabling interpretation of symptoms, clinical findings, or disease relationships, while decomposing diagnosis into explicit, auditable reasoning steps. This ontology-based grounding constrains inference to evidence-backed associations, reducing hallucination and improving diagnostic transparency, traceability, and consistency. The system then identifies the most discriminative missing symptoms and generates targeted follow-up questions to reduce uncertainty through a process that mirrors to clinical inquiry. Together, these components improve the reliability, explainability, and diagnostic accuracy of AI-assisted differential diagnosis. The source code is publicly available.

infographic.key_insight: An ontology-guided multi-agent framework makes differential diagnosis more traceable by grounding inference in curated medical knowledge and explicit reasoning steps.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help clinicians inspect diagnostic rationales and identify missing information through targeted follow-up questions.
method: Ground symptom, finding, and disease relationships in an expert-curated medical ontology.
Decompose diagnostic inference into explicit, auditable multi-agent reasoning steps.
Identify discriminative missing symptoms and generate targeted follow-up questions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports publicly available source code but provides no dataset details, evaluation metrics, or quantitative results supporting its claimed improvements.
infographic.watch_item: Reliability may depend on ontology coverage and quality; clinical utility requires validation beyond the claims in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promise in specialty medicine, yet existing evaluations largely focus on isolated clinical encounters rather than tracking how clinical responsibilities evolve across a longitudinal care pathway. Here we introduce NPC-RubricBench, a phase-aware benchmark for evaluating multistage clinical reasoning across the cancer care continuum, using nasopharyngeal carcinoma as a defined disease context. Curated from longitudinal records of 405 patients across two cancer centers, the benchmark comprises 941 patient-phase units across six sequential care phases and 17,688 patient-specific atomic criteria spanning five evaluation dimensions, with each assessment strictly restricted to decision-time clinical evidence. Evaluating 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs revealed that strong diagnostic performance does not carry over to downstream care. We evaluated 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs, showing that high diagnostic performance did not translate into improved downstream care. Instead, the dominant failure modes reversed across phases. Explicit decision errors dominated anatomical staging at 48.2%, whereas decision omissions dominated initial work-up and post-treatment follow-up at 33.4% and 30.4%, respectively. In the evaluated model set, medically adapted models showed higher omission rates than general-purpose models. Moreover, varying query granularity exposes a critical specification trade-off: broad open-ended requests degrade Decision Quality across all 30 models, while more detailed, checklist-like prompts raise Decision Quality but reduce Evidence Faithfulness and Safety Adherence. Furthermore, NPC-RubricBench demonstrates that static diagnostic benchmarks are insufficient to ensure consistent clinical reliability over time, highlighting the importance of phase-adaptive safeguards in multistage medical AI.

infographic.key_insight: Across 30 LLMs, strong diagnostic performance did not translate into reliable downstream cancer care, and dominant error types shifted by care phase.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Evaluating medical AI across the full care pathway may reveal omissions and decision errors missed by diagnosis-only benchmarks.
method: Built NPC-RubricBench from longitudinal nasopharyngeal carcinoma records at two cancer centers.
Evaluated 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs across six care phases using patient-specific criteria and decision-time evidence only.
Compared broad requests with detailed, checklist-like prompts.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark included 405 patients, 941 patient-phase units, and 17,688 criteria; explicit decision errors dominated anatomical staging (48.2%), while omissions dominated initial work-up (33.4%) and post-treatment follow-up (30.4%).
infographic.watch_item: Detailed prompts improved Decision Quality but reduced Evidence Faithfulness and Safety Adherence, highlighting a trade-off that requires validation before clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care

title: PathKGen: Pathology Knowledge Assisted MLLM for Explainable Histopathology
authors: Nadun Rajapaksha, Sandun Herath, Devnith Wijesinghe, Isiri Amani Withanawasam, Hasindri Watawana, Ranga Rodrigo
abstract: Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis serves as the fundamental method for the clinical diagnosis of cancer in digital histopathology. Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have enabled state-of-the-art (SOTA) automated histopathology report generation. However, MLLMs reason purely through distributions encoded in their neural parameters, limiting the amount of knowledge and reasoning logic they can contain given the model scale. Their black-box reasoning poses another challenge to the human interpretation of intermediate reasoning. We address these issues by utilizing knowledge graphs to inject external structured knowledge for MLLMs to reason over, while making this reasoning component visible. Knowledge graphs are capable of partially externalizing the containment of medical knowledge, an area that remains underexplored in pathology report generation. We introduce PathKGen, a knowledge graph-assisted MLLM for histopathology report generation. PathKGen has two main branches: (1) a visual path that learns visual token inputs to the MLLM using pathology foundation models, and (2) a knowledge path that learns knowledge token inputs by extracting key morphological features of WSIs through querying a pathology-specific knowledge graph. A comprehensive evaluation on WSI-Bench dataset shows that PathKGen surpasses previous SOTA methods while revealing diagnostic reasoning as visually intuitive graphs. Due to its modular design, the proposed knowledge path is complementary to vision-aligned MLLMs and can be extended to other applications by curating domain-specific knowledge graphs to generate knowledge tokens.

infographic.key_insight: PathKGen combines whole-slide image features with structured pathology knowledge to generate histopathology reports and expose part of its reasoning as graphs.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support more interpretable automated pathology reporting, but clinical usefulness and safety are not established by the abstract.
method: A visual branch uses pathology foundation models to produce image-derived tokens.
A knowledge branch queries a pathology-specific knowledge graph to produce morphology-based knowledge tokens.
A multimodal large language model uses both token streams for report generation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On WSI-Bench, the authors report performance exceeding previous state-of-the-art methods, but the abstract provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Reasoning graphs reveal only part of the process and do not establish that generated reports are correct.
infographic.paper_title: PathKGen: Pathology Knowledge Assisted MLLM for Explainable Histopathology

title: Cholesterol Paradox: Multi-point Heart Failure Prediction from Lipid Panels in Electronic Health Records
authors: Hou, Y.; Bhuiyan, M. K.; Samad, M.
abstract: In cardiovascular medicine, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is the main lipid marker used in routine screening to assess cardiovascular risk and guide preventive treatment and dietary changes. An increasing number of studies have recently documented the cholesterol paradox: patients with or at risk of heart failure (HF) often have unexpectedly low levels of LDL-C despite leading to cardiovascular diseases. This paper examines how well retrospective lipid panel measurements, supplemented with apolipoprotein B (ApoB), can predict an initial heart failure (HF) event in several pre-diagnosis time windows, using age-matched patient data from Electronic Health Records (EHRs). This retrospective study uses lipid profiles from multicenter nationwide EHRs from the All of Us Research Program. We apply machine learning and explainable AI (SHAP) to lipid-based prediction and to interpret cholesterol contributions to the diagnosis of first heart failure (HF). One experiment predicts the diagnosis of HF in 36 months; the other distinguishes HF patients from people who have never been diagnosed with cardiovascular disease. A baseline lipid panel that includes ApoB predicts the first HF event up to 36 months in advance, achieving an AUC of 0.624 in men and 0.627 in women. Compared to a group of the same age without previous cardiovascular disease, a lipid profile including ApoB predicts a first HF event with a substantially higher AUC: 0.937 for men and 0.925 for women. Shapley value analyses suggest that higher triglycerides and lower HDL and LDL levels are linked to subsequent HF events, with LDL appearing as the strongest yet counterintuitive predictor. ApoB ranks second in importance; in males, higher ApoB is associated with a greater risk of HF, unlike LDL. In general, the study highlights an unexpected association with LDL and emphasizes the prognostic utility of sex-specific metabolic indicators (TG, HDL) for HF using routinely collected clinical data.

infographic.key_insight: Lipid profiles including ApoB predicted first heart failure events, with lower LDL emerging as the strongest counterintuitive predictor.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Routine lipid measurements may offer sex-specific signals of future heart failure, but these associations do not establish causality or justify changing cholesterol treatment.
method: Retrospective analysis of age-matched, multicenter All of Us electronic health records.
Machine learning using lipid panels plus ApoB to predict first heart failure across pre-diagnosis windows.
SHAP analysis to interpret lipid contributions and sex-specific patterns.
infographic.evidence_signal: Up to 36 months before first heart failure, AUC was 0.624 in men and 0.627 in women; comparison with age-matched people never diagnosed with cardiovascular disease yielded AUCs of 0.937 and 0.925, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depended strongly on the comparison group, so the high AUCs against cardiovascular-disease-free controls should not be interpreted as equivalent to prospective clinical prediction.
infographic.paper_title: Cholesterol Paradox: Multi-point Heart Failure Prediction from Lipid Panels in Electronic Health Records

title: Evaluating Federated Vision-Language and Vision-Only Models for Privacy-Aware Breast Cancer Imaging
authors: Malithi Mithsara Wanniarachchi Kankanamge, Ning Yang, Sree Bash Debnath, Md Zobaer Islam, Abdur R. Shahid
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) shows promise for breast imaging, but limited labeled data, institutional data fragmentation, and privacy concerns hinder centralized training. We investigate a privacy-aware federated learning framework combining pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with client-level differential privacy. We compare general-purpose CLIP models, biomedical BiomedCLIP, and an ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 baseline on two public breast imaging datasets, with and without differential privacy. We also evaluate a CLIP ViT-B/16 ablation that removes the text pathway. Evaluation includes patient-level ROC-AUC with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, baseline comparisons, threshold sensitivity, inter-model agreement, and communication cost. Under federated learning, all five models achieve high normal-versus-sick discrimination (ROC-AUC: 0.940-0.990). However, acquisition year alone achieves 0.974 on the same test partition, raising concerns about confounding rather than genuine pathology recognition. Benign-versus-malignant discrimination remains uncertain (ROC-AUC: 0.504-0.637), with all confidence intervals including 0.50. Removing the text pathway preserves classification accuracy while halving communication cost. Differential privacy reduces ROC-AUC by 0.375, attributable to perturbing the full model state rather than only trainable parameters. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating confounding, predictive reliability, privacy implementation, and deployment efficiency when developing federated AI systems for breast imaging.

infographic.key_insight: Federated models showed high normal-versus-sick discrimination, but acquisition-year confounding challenges whether they learned genuine pathology signals.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings support further validation—not clinical use—before relying on federated breast-imaging AI to distinguish benign from malignant findings.
method: Compared CLIP, BiomedCLIP, and an ImageNet-pretrained ViT across two public breast-imaging datasets.
Evaluated federated training with and without client-level differential privacy.
Tested a text-free CLIP ablation and assessed patient-level performance, agreement, and communication cost.
infographic.evidence_signal: Normal-versus-sick ROC-AUC was 0.940–0.990 versus 0.974 for acquisition year alone; benign-versus-malignant ROC-AUC was 0.504–0.637, with all bootstrap 95% confidence intervals including 0.50.
infographic.watch_item: Differential privacy reduced ROC-AUC by 0.375, attributed to perturbing the full model state rather than only trainable parameters.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluating Federated Vision-Language and Vision-Only Models for Privacy-Aware Breast Cancer Imaging

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
abstract: Recently, there has been rise in multimodal vision-language models for computer-aided diagnosis (CAD), yet their application in breast diagnosis, particularly for predicting biopsy outcomes remains limited. This study presents a multimodal vision-language approach, incorporating Grad-CAM as an Explainable AI (XAI) technique, to predict benign tumors in patients recommended for biopsy, especially those classified as BI-RADS 4 and 5. A novel multimodal framework was devel- oped using Vision Transformer (ViT) for imaging feature extraction and DeBERTa-V3-Large for textual embeddings. The model was trained and evaluated on a comprehensive in-house dataset comprising 1,632 patients, each with four mammography views and a corresponding radiology report. The features of both modalities were extracted independently and fused by late fusion before classification. Grad-CAM was used to generate visual explanations highlighting key regions influencing model predictions. The proposed model demonstrated high sensitivity 90%, 95%, 99%, and 100% with corresponding specificities of 40%, 36%, 18%, and 11%, respectively. The best AUC achieved was 0.72 by multimodal approach on the test set, outperforming the image only (0.66) and text-only (0.68) baselines. The proposed multimodal architecture, enhanced with Grad-CAM, demonstrates a strong potential to identify benign tumors among high-risk patients, offering interpretable insights and thereby helping reduce unnecessary biopsies, patient anxiety, and healthcare costs.

infographic.key_insight: Combining mammograms and radiology reports improved biopsy-outcome discrimination over either modality alone, with a test AUC of 0.72.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help identify benign findings among patients recommended for biopsy, particularly BI-RADS 4–5, but clinical benefit remains unproven.
method: Vision Transformer extracted features from four mammography views per patient.
DeBERTa-V3-Large encoded radiology reports; late fusion combined image and text features.
Grad-CAM highlighted image regions influencing predictions.
infographic.evidence_signal: On an in-house dataset of 1,632 patients, test AUC was 0.72 versus 0.66 for images alone and 0.68 for text alone; specificity was 18% at 99% sensitivity.
infographic.watch_item: External validation and prospective safety assessment are needed before using predictions to defer biopsies.
infographic.paper_title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
abstract: Clinical expertise is inherently distributed: it resides not in any single dataset or institution but in the accumulated reasoning experiences of thousands of clinicians navigating diverse patient populations, resource constraints, and evolving treatment protocols. Yet current approaches to scaling medical AI, from centralized large language models to federated learning, remain anchored to a data-centric paradigm that treats knowledge as static parameters to be aggregated. In this Perspective, we argue for a fundamental shift from data aggregation to experience aggregation. We propose Decentralized Agentic Systems (DAS), a framework in which distributed AI agents operating across healthcare institutions synthesize collective clinical intelligence by sharing abstracted reasoning trajectories rather than raw data or model parameters. Unlike federated learning, which averages numerical gradients across homogeneous model architectures, DAS exchanges structured records of clinical reasoning, specifically the sequence of observations, hypotheses, tool invocations, and outcome feedback that constitute diagnostic experience. We examine the architectural principles, deployment considerations, governance requirements, and critical open challenges of this framework, laying the groundwork for a collaborative medical AI ecosystem where distributed expertise autonomously adapts to the complexities of longitudinal patient care.

infographic.key_insight: This Perspective proposes Decentralized Agentic Systems (DAS) that share structured reasoning experiences across institutions rather than raw data or model parameters.
infographic.clinical_relevance: DAS could help medical AI learn from diverse institutional experiences and adapt to longitudinal patient care, but clinical benefits remain unproven.
method: Connect distributed AI agents across healthcare institutions.
Exchange abstracted trajectories of observations, hypotheses, tool use, and outcome feedback.
Aggregate reasoning experiences to build collective clinical intelligence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a conceptual framework and discusses deployment and governance; it reports no datasets, empirical evaluations, or clinical outcomes.
infographic.watch_item: Sharing reasoning trajectories requires safeguards against disclosure of sensitive patient information.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence

title: OA-RAG: Ontology-based Agentic RAG for Faithful LLM Reasoning
authors: Hui Yang, Jiaoyan Chen, Yongsheng Gao
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well across many real-world tasks but remain prone to hallucination, limiting their reliability in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare, where answers must be grounded in established knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates this problem by incorporating external information, but often overlooks logical relationships and relies heavily on the LLM's own reasoning, which can compromise answer faithfulness. We propose OA-RAG, an agent that integrates formal reasoning with LLM reasoning, drawing on both the logical structure and informal annotations of domain ontologies. For each answer, OA-RAG reports the ontology observations used as evidence and a model-assessed grounding level (entailed, supported, related, or unrelated) that characterises the strength of that evidence. Across benchmarks derived from three large-scale ontologies and six real-world medical question-answering tasks, OA-RAG achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated ontology-fine-tuned and popular RAG methods, with particularly strong results on reasoning-intensive tasks. The reported grounding levels also offer a useful indication of answer reliability, with stronger grounding generally associated with higher accuracy. Finally, our results demonstrate the value of ontologies as knowledge sources: OA-RAG is competitive with, and sometimes outperforms, domain-specific RAG systems that draw on sources such as textbooks.

infographic.key_insight: OA-RAG combines ontology-based formal reasoning with LLM reasoning to improve answer faithfulness and report the strength of supporting evidence.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could make medical question-answering systems more transparent, but the abstract does not establish safety or effectiveness in clinical care.
method: Retrieves logical relationships and descriptive annotations from domain ontologies.
Integrates formal reasoning with LLM reasoning through an agent.
Reports ontology evidence and model-assessed grounding: entailed, supported, related, or unrelated.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across benchmarks derived from three large-scale ontologies and six real-world medical QA tasks, OA-RAG achieved the best overall performance among evaluated methods, with stronger grounding generally associated with higher accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Grounding levels are model-assessed signals, not guarantees of correctness or clinical reliability.
infographic.paper_title: OA-RAG: Ontology-based Agentic RAG for Faithful LLM Reasoning

title: Identifying cohorts at elevated risk of cancers using generative modeling of patient health states
authors: Khan, A.; Forster, D. T.; Harsh, M.; Zheng, C.; Warner, E. T.; Ritter, D.; Chang, A.; Wei, Q.; Sorensen, T. K.; Marks, D. S.; Sequist, L. V.; Hadlock, J. J.; Fillmore, N. R.; Sander, C.
abstract: While large language models are powerful generators of new text, forecasting disease progression from longitudinal health histories remains a challenging problem. We introduce GenEHR, an autoregressive generative model trained on electronic health records (EHRs) from millions of patients in diverse health systems. The model learns from real-world multimodal patient histories, including diagnoses, medications, lab values, and procedures while explicitly representing irregular intervals between visits to forecast future clinical events. We combine the general-purpose patient representation learned during foundational training with parameter-efficient supervised adaptation for the task of risk stratification for 17 cancer types. In five large EHR cohorts, supervised adaptation substantially improved prediction performance of a first cancer diagnosis within a five year horizon window. Our retrospective results support the prospective evaluation of GenEHR-CancerRisk as a clinical decision-support tool for prioritizing high-risk patients for screening and prevention of aggressive cancer types, such as pancreatic and ovarian cancer.

infographic.key_insight: GenEHR combines generative modeling of patient histories with supervised adaptation to identify cohorts at elevated risk of a first cancer diagnosis within five years.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help prioritize high-risk patients for screening and prevention, but its clinical utility requires prospective evaluation.
method: Train an autoregressive model on longitudinal EHRs from millions of patients.
Model diagnoses, medications, lab values, procedures, and irregular intervals between visits.
Use parameter-efficient supervised adaptation for risk stratification across 17 cancer types.
infographic.evidence_signal: Retrospective evaluation in five large EHR cohorts found that supervised adaptation substantially improved five-year cancer prediction performance; the abstract reports no numerical metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Prospective validation is needed to establish whether risk-guided screening improves outcomes without excessive false positives or unnecessary procedures.
infographic.paper_title: Identifying cohorts at elevated risk of cancers using generative modeling of patient health states

title: When uncertainty quantification fails: structural vulnerabilities and corrections for selective prediction under clinical class imbalance
authors: Walter Endrizzi, Flavio Ragni, Raffaele Marchesi, Stefano Bovo, Monica Moroni, Giuseppe Jurman
abstract: Background. Selective prediction systems improve the safety of clinical artificial intelligence by deferring ambiguous cases to human experts while automating high-confidence decisions. However, this safety mechanism relies entirely on the premise that uncertainty scores accurately reflect clinical ambiguity. In prognostic tasks characterized by severe class imbalance, where the clinical outcome of interest is a minority, this assumption breaks down. Standard uncertainty measures cease to capture clinically aligned ambiguity; instead, they become a proxy for class membership, systematically penalizing minority patients regardless of their individual predictive clarity. Results. Across 56 synthetic conditions and three neurodegenerative cohorts spanning severe class imbalance to near-balanced conditions (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's Disease, Alzheimer's Disease), our framework consistently maintained bounded, balanced risk across trajectories. In contrast, global metrics either collapsed minority Sensitivity or protected the minority at the expense of majority patients. Applying CCR with standard entropy fails to protect the minority because it breaks within-class monotonicity when tau=0.5. Combining CCR with threshold-aware metrics restores strict monotonicity, correctly identifies ambiguous patients, and safely mitigates minority exclusion. Conclusions. Under clinical class imbalance, standard uncertainty quantification measures dataset sparsity rather than clinical ambiguity, creating a systemic illusion of safety. This bias is a correctable structural flaw. Clinical pipelines deploying selective prediction under imbalance should adopt threshold-aligned uncertainty measures and class-stratified evaluation. This reduces class-specific risk imbalance, supporting safer selective prediction under the evaluated conditions without silently excluding the most vulnerable patients.

infographic.key_insight: Under class imbalance, standard uncertainty scores can track class membership rather than ambiguity, undermining the safety of selective prediction.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Threshold-aligned uncertainty and class-stratified evaluation may help clinical AI defer ambiguous cases without disproportionately excluding minority-outcome patients.
method: Evaluated selective prediction across varying degrees of class imbalance.
Compared standard uncertainty measures with threshold-aware alternatives.
Combined CCR with threshold-aware metrics to restore within-class monotonicity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 56 synthetic conditions and three neurodegenerative cohorts covering multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, and Alzheimer’s disease, the proposed framework maintained bounded, balanced risk under the evaluated conditions.
infographic.watch_item: The reported evaluations do not establish prospective clinical safety; implementation requires validating thresholds and class-specific risk in the intended population.
infographic.paper_title: When uncertainty quantification fails: structural vulnerabilities and corrections for selective prediction under clinical class imbalance

title: Acute Stroke Classification Using Asymmetric Data Standardization and Orthogonal-Focal Loss Optimized CNN-ViT Cross-Attention Fusion: A Multicenter External Validation Study
authors: Tansel Uyar
abstract: Background/Objectives: Rapid differentiation of ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke subtypes is vital for acute management. Although current deep learning models achieve high single-dataset accuracy, they suffer from "shortcut learning" and domain shift in external validation. This study proposes a hierarchical computer-aided diagnostic (CAD) system mimicking emergency triage. Methods: We introduce a 3-channel Radiology-Focused Preprocessing pipeline that feeds radiological Hounsfield Unit (HU) windows into Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Vision Transformer (ViT) backbones via asymmetric formats (.mat and .png). The architecture utilizes a novel joint cross-attention fusion network optimized by an Integrated Orthogonal-Focal Loss. Results: Our system achieved a 95.48% F1-score on the internal stroke dataset. However, multi-center external validation (AISD, BHSD, PhysioNet) using a Mask Anchor filter revealed a drop to the 58-62% range, exposing the "internal validation illusion" caused by hardware noise. Critically, models exhibited high precision (77%) but low sensitivity (57%) for ischemic stroke, proving prone to hemorrhage overdiagnosis. Multi-seed variance analysis demonstrated that the DenseNet201+ViT backbone yielded the lowest deviation (0.59) and highest stability, making it the most reliable architecture for real-world clinical integration. Conclusions: To overcome diagnostic challenges, future research must focus on multimodal architectures that combine 3D volumetric extraction with clinical data.

infographic.key_insight: Strong internal stroke-classification performance did not generalize across centers, with F1 falling from 95.48% to approximately 58–62% on external validation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Low ischemic-stroke sensitivity and a tendency toward hemorrhage overdiagnosis raise concerns about reliability in acute stroke triage.
method: Three-channel CT preprocessing used radiological Hounsfield Unit windows in asymmetric .mat and .png formats.
CNN and Vision Transformer features were combined through cross-attention fusion.
Training used Integrated Orthogonal-Focal Loss; evaluation included external datasets and multi-seed stability analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: External evaluation on AISD, BHSD, and PhysioNet using a Mask Anchor filter showed reduced performance, with reported ischemic-stroke precision of 77% and sensitivity of 57%.
infographic.watch_item: DenseNet201+ViT showed the lowest multi-seed variability, but stability alone does not establish clinical readiness given the external performance gap.
infographic.paper_title: Acute Stroke Classification Using Asymmetric Data Standardization and Orthogonal-Focal Loss Optimized CNN-ViT Cross-Attention Fusion: A Multicenter External Validation Study

title: Evaluating Bayesian deep learning for robust biomedical time-series classification under distribution shift: A sleep scoring case study
authors: Mads Birch Sørensen, Ulrike Richter, Francois Gastambide, Michael Riis Andersen
abstract: In biomedical time-series classification, machine learning models often suffer from deteriorating accuracy and calibration due to distribution shift. We investigate to what degree Bayesian-inspired deep learning improves robustness through Bayesian model averaging (BMA). Using rodent sleep scoring as a case study, we evaluate BMA under distribution shifts in genotype, laboratory, and species. We systematically compare nine approximate inference methods spanning single- and multi-basin approaches across two neural network backbones on in-distribution (ID) data and five out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets. In our results, multi-basin methods perform best, outperforming baselines and single-basin methods. Compared with point estimates, BMA generally improves OOD accuracy and calibration across both architectures, while yielding only modest ID gains. It also often improves selective prediction and OOD and artifact detection, but, interestingly, not inter-rater disagreement detection.

infographic.key_insight: Bayesian model averaging generally improved accuracy and calibration under distribution shift in rodent sleep scoring, with multi-basin methods performing best.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The findings may inform more robust biomedical time-series classifiers, but do not establish performance or clinical utility in human sleep scoring.
method: Compared nine approximate Bayesian inference methods spanning single- and multi-basin approaches.
Evaluated two neural network backbones against point-estimate baselines.
Tested shifts in genotype, laboratory, and species.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation used in-distribution data and five out-of-distribution datasets, finding modest in-distribution gains and generally improved out-of-distribution accuracy and calibration.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits were not universal: Bayesian model averaging did not improve inter-rater disagreement detection.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluating Bayesian deep learning for robust biomedical time-series classification under distribution shift: A sleep scoring case study

title: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents
authors: Hannes Ill, Rafi Al Attrach, Rajna Fani, Ahram Han, Ryohei Yamamoto, Marlene Louisa Moerig
abstract: Clinical research over electronic health records depends on derived variables whose definitions sit outside the schema, in item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output-grain choices that change cohorts and downstream conclusions. We introduce M4Bench, 28 clinical derivation tasks across 15 task families on MIMIC-IV and eICU, to test whether AI coding agents can reproduce such derivations and how clinician-reviewed agent skills change their results. Its controls decompose the value of skills into specification completeness, delivery format, and schema familiarity. In a Docker-isolated Codex campaign (GPT 5.4 Mini and GPT 5.5), skills raise reward by 0.136 over the no-skill baseline, with 26 of 28 tasks improving. Specification completeness accounts for most of this gain: on an eight-task control subset, an operational spec alone raises reward by 0.162, and skills add only 0.024 on top, indistinguishable from zero. On a ten-task subset, decoy skills score like no skill and raw reference SQL nearly matches targeted skills, arguing against generic context or the skill format as the explanation. Schema obfuscation and restructuring preserve 86% and 70% of the skill gain (GPT 5.4 Mini, 26 MIMIC-IV tasks), a descriptive robustness check rather than a bound on memorization. A descriptive Claude Code replication on all 28 tasks (Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6, 560 runs) is directionally consistent (+0.120, 21 of 28 tasks improving). These gains are partial agreement with the reference, not completed tasks: only 25 of 280 with-skill and 13 of 280 no-skill Codex runs pass every strict check, and skills barely change which rows agents return (key F1 +0.003). Skills are released as a versioned, clinician-reviewable markdown delivery format, with a family-level reference-validity audit. M4Bench releases tasks, skills, evaluation code, and sanitized per-run evidence as an open-source benchmark.

infographic.key_insight: Complete procedural specifications—not the skill format itself—accounted for most gains in AI agents’ agreement with reference clinical EHR derivations.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Explicit rules for codes, time windows, missingness, and output granularity may improve reproducibility of EHR research variables, but agent outputs still require validation.
method: Benchmarked 28 clinical derivation tasks across 15 task families on MIMIC-IV and eICU.
Compared clinician-reviewed skills with no skills, operational specifications, decoy skills, and reference SQL.
Tested schema changes and conducted a descriptive replication with Claude Code.
infographic.evidence_signal: In Codex evaluation, skills increased reward by 0.136, with 26 of 28 tasks improving; only 25 of 280 with-skill runs passed every strict check, versus 13 of 280 without skills.
infographic.watch_item: Higher reward reflected partial reference agreement, not reliable task completion; skills barely improved which rows agents returned.
infographic.paper_title: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents

title: OpenGray: a benchmark for evaluating the decisions of radiotherapy planning agents
authors: Humza Nusrat, Kundan Thind
abstract: Background and purpose: Radiotherapy planning agents based on large language models (LLMs) decide when to submit a plan or request review but are evaluated mainly by dose. This study developed OpenGray, a benchmark of planning tasks with known correct decisions. Materials and methods: OpenGray adds tasks with known answers to the OpenKBP-Opt head-and-neck dataset, including two contradictions with dose goals proven incompatible and a feasible control with a stored plan meeting every hard goal. Four systems, from a rule-based planning script to a full LLM agent, were evaluated on 30 patients, the LLM-based ones with a commercial (Terra) and a local (Ministral 3 8B) LLM. Decisions, achieved dose, problem recognition, and technical failures were recorded and also read from logs of 39 stereotactic radiosurgery runs of SAGE, a clinical LLM agent. Results: With Terra, the script preceded by an LLM review and the full agent had decision accuracies of 95.4% and 92.1%, respectively, yet escalated only 50% (95% confidence interval, 25-75%) and 25% (10-40%) of overlap contradictions, which required arithmetic on the anatomy. All four systems submitted every feasible control, but 24% of these plans missed a hard goal that the stored plan had met. In four SAGE runs, one goal failed at every attempt; the agent identified it in every reply but had no action for stopping. Conclusions: Favorable aggregate scores concealed specific decision failures. Planning agents should be evaluated on their decisions as well as their dose and given an explicit action for stopping and requesting review.

infographic.key_insight: High overall decision accuracy concealed failures to escalate incompatible radiotherapy goals, while some submitted plans missed achievable hard goals.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Evaluating when AI planning agents submit, stop, or request review may reveal safety-relevant failures that dose metrics alone miss.
method: Built OpenGray with provably incompatible dose goals and feasible controls backed by stored plans.
Evaluated four planning systems on 30 head-and-neck patients, using commercial and local LLMs.
Examined decisions, dose, problem recognition, and technical failures, plus logs from 39 SAGE radiosurgery runs.
infographic.evidence_signal: With Terra, two LLM-based systems achieved 95.4% and 92.1% decision accuracy but escalated only 50% and 25% of overlap contradictions; 24% of submitted feasible-control plans missed a hard goal.
infographic.watch_item: The small evaluation does not establish clinical safety; recognizing an unsatisfied goal also requires an explicit stop-and-review action.
infographic.paper_title: OpenGray: a benchmark for evaluating the decisions of radiotherapy planning agents

title: Reliability-Aware Short-Term Glycemic Risk Prediction Using an Anchor-Based Comparative Framework of Sequence, Multimodal, and State-Updating Digital-Twin Models
authors: Pir Bakhsh Khokhar, Carmine Gravino, Fabio Palomba
abstract: Anticipating short-term hypoglycemic and hyperglycemic risk is essential for proactive diabetes management. However, existing machine learning approaches often use inconsistent evaluation protocols and emphasize predictive performance over reliability. This study introduces an anchor-based benchmarking framework integrating longitudinal glucose sequences and multimodal patient information. Using the T1DiabetesGranada dataset, 5,503,441 standardized prediction anchors were constructed from 736 individuals with type 1 diabetes to evaluate hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia prediction at 30-, 60-, and 120-minute horizons. Three neural architectures, a Hybrid LSTM-Transformer, a Multimodal Digital Twin, and a State-Updating Digital Twin with gap-aware longitudinal state progression, were compared under identical patient-level validation protocols. Beyond predictive performance, the evaluation examined calibration, classification thresholds, explanation reliability, cross-model disagreement, and robustness to controlled perturbations. No statistically significant predictive differences were observed after Holm correction, although the models exhibited complementary reliability characteristics. The Multimodal Digital Twin achieved the lowest mean Brier score, while the State-Updating Digital Twin demonstrated the lowest mean expected calibration error (ECE-10). The Hybrid LSTM-Transformer showed strong explanation faithfulness and stability under its temporal attribution protocol. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating digital-twin models beyond predictive accuracy and emphasize the need for reliability assessment and external validation before clinical deployment.

infographic.key_insight: Three neural models showed no statistically significant predictive differences after Holm correction but had complementary strengths in calibration and explanation reliability.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Reliable short-term glucose-risk forecasts could support proactive type 1 diabetes management, but clinical deployment requires further validation.
method: Built standardized prediction anchors from longitudinal glucose and multimodal patient data.
Compared Hybrid LSTM-Transformer, Multimodal Digital Twin, and State-Updating Digital Twin models under identical patient-level validation.
Predicted hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia at 30, 60, and 120 minutes while assessing calibration, explanations, disagreement, and robustness.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation used 5,503,441 anchors from 736 individuals in T1DiabetesGranada; the Multimodal Digital Twin had the lowest mean Brier score, and the State-Updating Digital Twin had the lowest mean ECE-10.
infographic.watch_item: Results from one dataset need external validation before generalizability and clinical readiness can be established.
infographic.paper_title: Reliability-Aware Short-Term Glycemic Risk Prediction Using an Anchor-Based Comparative Framework of Sequence, Multimodal, and State-Updating Digital-Twin Models

title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Liver Lesion Segmentation and Structured Radiology Reporting
authors: Fatma Ahmed Mansour, Rahatara Ferdousi, Manar Fathy Elshenawy
abstract: Despite advances in automated liver lesion segmentation, a gap remains between image-derived predictions and clinically interpretable radiology reports. Bridging this gap requires quantitative measurements that are both reproducible and traceable. We present an evidence-grounded agentic AI framework that connects liver and lesion segmentation with deterministic quantification and structured reporting. TotalSegmentator-based nnU-Net models delineate the liver, Couinaud segments, and lesions, while computational tools extract volumes, dimensions, counts, and anatomical locations. A large language model (LLM) organizes these measurements into a predefined reporting schema, with numerical consistency checks against source measurements. On 51 LiTS cases, the segmentation stage achieved a liver Dice score of 0.947, lesion sensitivity of 75.6%, and positive predictive value of 68.9%. Exploratory screening of 25,494 MERLIN reports identified 10,208 (40.0%) with liver-related abnormalities. By connecting quantitative imaging evidence with agentic report generation, this work takes a step toward human-centered medical AI that prioritizes traceability and clinical relevance.

infographic.key_insight: An agentic AI workflow links liver lesion segmentation to structured radiology reports using traceable measurements and numerical consistency checks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help translate imaging predictions into interpretable reports, but clinical utility remains to be established.
method: TotalSegmentator-based nnU-Net models segment the liver, Couinaud segments, and lesions.
Deterministic tools calculate volumes, dimensions, lesion counts, and anatomical locations.
An LLM organizes measurements into a predefined report schema with numerical consistency checks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 51 LiTS cases, liver Dice was 0.947, lesion sensitivity 75.6%, and positive predictive value 68.9%; separate exploratory screening found liver-related abnormalities in 10,208 of 25,494 MERLIN reports (40.0%).
infographic.watch_item: Incomplete lesion detection and false positives warrant expert review; the abstract does not report end-to-end clinical validation of generated reports.
infographic.paper_title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Liver Lesion Segmentation and Structured Radiology Reporting
